content: There is an urgent need to develop systematic and effective solutions to address inefficiencies in healthcare systems and to promote the rational use of health technologies. Independent health intervention and technology assessments play a critical role as multidisciplinary policy research tools. These assessments generate evidence to guide the prioritization, selection, introduction, distribution, and management of health interventions aimed at health promotion, disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative care. By employing rigorous research methodologies and transparent, inclusive processes, the evaluation of medicines, vaccines, medical devices, equipment, and health procedures—including preventive interventions—can provide reliable information on their safety, efficacy, quality, appropriateness, cost-effectiveness, and efficiency. This information is essential for determining whether and when these technologies should be integrated into specific health interventions and systems. However, in many developing countries, the capacity to assess, research, and document the public health, economic, organizational, social, legal, and ethical implications of health interventions and technologies is inadequate. This results in insufficient information to guide rational policy-making, professional decisions, and clinical practices. Recognizing the importance of strengthening national capacity, regional and international networking, and collaboration in health intervention and technology assessment, the following actions are urged: 1. Member States are encouraged to establish national systems for health intervention and technology assessment. These systems should systematically utilize independent assessments to support universal health coverage and inform policy decisions, including priority-setting, selection, procurement, supply chain management, and the use of health interventions and technologies. They should also aid in the development of sustainable financing packages, pharmaceutical formularies, clinical practice guidelines, and protocols for public health programs. 2. 3. In addition to established methods, Member States are encouraged to develop national guidelines and monitoring systems for health intervention and technology assessment. 4. Efforts should be made to integrate and promote health intervention and technology assessment within national frameworks, such as those for health system research, professional education, health system strengthening, and universal health coverage. 5. Member States should enhance national capacity for regional and international networking, develop local expertise, avoid duplication of efforts, and optimize resource utilization. 6. Collaboration with other Member States, health organizations, academic institutions, professional associations, and key stakeholders is encouraged to share information, lessons learned, and best practices. This will support the formulation and implementation of national strategic plans for capacity-building and the introduction of health intervention and technology assessment. 7. Gaps in promoting and implementing evidence-based health policy should be identified, along with improvements in information systems and research capacity. Member States are encouraged to seek technical support and exchange information and experiences with other countries, regional networks, and international entities, including the World Health Organization (WHO). 8. Data collection on health intervention and technology assessment should be improved, and relevant professionals should be trained to enhance assessment capacity. The Director-General of WHO is requested to: 1. Assess the status of health intervention and technology assessment in Member States, including methodology, human resources, institutional capacity, governance, and the linkage between assessment units and policy authorities. This includes evaluating the use of assessment results and identifying barriers to strengthening capacity. 2. Raise awareness, foster knowledge, and promote the practice of health intervention and technology assessment among national policymakers and stakeholders. This includes sharing best practices from competent research institutions and assessment agencies through global and regional networks. 3. 4. Provide technical support to Member States, particularly low-income countries, to strengthen their capacity for health intervention and technology assessment. This includes developing and using global guidance on methods and processes based on internationally agreed practices. 5. 6. Support the exchange of information, sharing of experiences, and capacity-building in health intervention and technology assessment through collaborative mechanisms and networks at global, regional, and national levels. These partnerships should be active, effective, and sustainable. 7. Report on the progress of implementing this resolution to the Sixty-ninth World Health Assembly.
